bivy.name: Thornton Pass benches
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and effectively the only base for this route: flat rock-and-heather benches on the ridge crest just south of the pass. Parties take most of a day to reach it — around seven and a half hours of brush and cliff-band navigation from the trailhead — and then run the whole climb as an enormous out-and-back from here. It is a crest site, so wind is the trade for the flat ground. Water is the real constraint: fill at Thornton Creek low on the approach, because by late summer the snow patches near the benches can be gone. Summit day commonly ends after dark, and finding these benches again in the dark is the crux of the return; the published alternative is a cold night out on the talus, which is an outcome to plan against rather than a site.
bivy.water: lingering snow patches only — no reliable stream at camp
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: a few tents on separate benches

bivy.name: Upper Despair Lake
bivy.notes: NOT a documented camp — reports use it as a rest and water stop on the long traverse to the peak, and no established sites are described there. It is the last reliable water before the cliff band below the southeast face, and worth knowing about as an EMERGENCY stopping point if a party is benighted on the traverse rather than as a planned camp. Snow patches and steep chutes linger around the Despair Lakes into early summer.
bivy.water: the lake
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips

bivy.name: Access Creek Basin
bivy.notes: Where the Access Creek bushwhack finally lets go of you and opens onto talus, roughly 1,900 ft above the Big Beaver crossing. Parties reaching it late on day one commonly reported arriving around 7pm. It is the last water before the long, shadeless scree chute to Access Col, and the usual place to stash bushwhacking gear and spare fuel before going high. Not a pretty camp — deadfall, brush and biting insects — but flat, watered and low, which is what matters after devil's club and huckleberry. Coming out, it is also the target that keeps the descent from turning into an epic.
bivy.water: Access Creek runs through the basin, plus meltwater off the snow above it; dependable all season
bivy.permit: Overnight camping anywhere inside North Cascades National Park needs a National Park Service backcountry permit, and cross-country camps must be on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows, and at least 100 ft back from water
bivy.capacity: Open talus and brush with room for a small party — parties describe picking a flat patch rather than using established sites

bivy.name: Luna Col (Luna Pass)
bivy.notes: The high camp for summit day, reached after the notorious steep heather-and-talus traverse from Access Col. The ground is glacier-polished slab with very little truly flat tent space, so most parties bivy rather than pitch. Being a saddle, it takes wind from either side with nothing to hide behind — one party woke at midnight to their cook pot being blown around, and got rain and blown grit before dawn. From here the Direct East Ridge still means dropping east, a long traverse around the 6,300-6,600 ft level and an ascending traverse to the 7,050 ft notch, so this is the only shelter you will see until you are back.
bivy.water: A snow patch sitting at the saddle is the only supply; it shrinks through the summer, so late-season parties should expect a shallow melt pool or nothing at all
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required; the col sits in the Luna cross-country zone, which the park caps at six people per party and six parties per night
bivy.capacity: A scatter of small bivy platforms among rock windbreaks — reports describe several cramped spots and only one genuinely comfortable one

bivy.name: Luna Col (Luna Pass)
bivy.notes: The standard high camp and the base for summit day on Fury, reached after a long steep heather-and-talus traverse from Access Col. It is a planned camp but a rough one — glacially polished slabs with very few genuinely flat tent spots, so most parties bivy rather than pitch. Being a saddle it is fully wind-exposed with no shelter in any direction, and the water depends entirely on a snow patch that shrinks all summer, so check it rather than assume it. From here the summit involves several miles of ridge, a steep heather chute and a crevassed glacier, and this is the only sheltered ground you will come back to.
bivy.water: A small snowfield sitting right at the saddle normally gives running water; by late season it is down to a shallow snowmelt pool, and in a hot low-snow year it may be gone entirely
bivy.permit: Camping needs a National Park Service backcountry permit; the col lies in the Luna cross-country zone, capped at six people per party and six parties per night
bivy.capacity: A handful of bivy-sized spots on slabs and gravel; the Luna cross-country zone allows six parties a night, six people per party

bivy.name: Access Basin camp
bivy.notes: A planned camp used to break the approach, at the head of Access Creek where the bushwhack finally opens onto talus. It is the last water before the long, hot, shadeless scree chute up to Access Col, and it is where most parties stash anything not needed above. It is not scenic or comfortable — brush, deadfall and biting insects — but it is flat, watered and low, which is the whole point after roughly 1,900 ft of devil's club and huckleberry. Coming down off the mountain, this is the target that turns an epic back into a walk out.
bivy.water: Access Creek runs through the basin, and there is meltwater below the snowfields above it; reliable through the season
bivy.permit: Overnight camping requires a National Park Service backcountry permit
bivy.capacity: Open talus and brush ground with room for a small party; a flat-topped boulder is a known sleeping spot

bivy.name: Lower Depot Creek bench
bivy.notes: Where the valley flattens and opens out above the Depot Creek Falls headwall. Parties use it two ways: as a shorter first day when the falls have taken longer than expected, and on the way out to put an hour of walking behind them. From here a scramble up and left onto the big buttress is a shortcut toward the Redoubt Glacier.
bivy.water: Depot Creek, alongside.
bivy.permit: Inside North Cascades National Park, so an overnight needs a wilderness permit; cross-country camping is allowed only on durable surfaces and not in meadows or within 100 ft of water.
bivy.capacity: Not published — informal ground rather than an established site.

bivy.name: Ouzel Lake
bivy.notes: The standard high camp and the one that serves both Spickard and Redoubt, on flat sandy treeless benches and a gravel moraine at the head of the valley below the calving front of the Redoubt Glacier. Six to nine hours and roughly 3,300 ft from the road, and the crux of getting here is the Depot Creek Falls headwall — over 900 ft of wet, slippery ground with a greasy rock step, where parties have found fixed hand lines at the two vertical sections. That headwall, not the distance, is why the lower bench gets used. Despite the route's name, the line turns off well before the pass that leads to Silver Lake and never reaches it; Silver Lake is a camp on the separate Silver Creek approach from Ross Lake.
bivy.water: The lake and Depot Creek at its outlet — glacier-fed and milky, and it is not reported to fail. Some parties pitch a little above the outlet for easy access.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, walk-up only — the cross-country zones covering this approach, Depot and Spickard, cannot be reserved in advance. Both cap a party at six people; Depot issues six permits a night and Spickard three. Ask at the Wilderness Information Center which of the two your intended site falls in, because the boundary is often not stated. Camping is allowed only on durable ground and not within 100 ft of water. The approach begins in British Columbia and crosses the border on foot at the boundary monument, where there is a trail register; carry passports.
bivy.capacity: No published tent count; parties regularly find others already there. The number that actually binds is the permit cap of six people.

bivy.name: Thornton Lakes camp
bivy.notes: Where the maintained trail ends, about five and a half miles in, at the outlet of the lower lake. It is the easy, legal, reliable option and the one to take if you arrive late or the col is booked out — but it leaves a very long summit day, since the col is still a thousand-plus feet of steep talus and grass above you. Most parties climbing the ridge push past it.
bivy.water: The outlet of the lower lake, immediately at the sites.
bivy.permit: A National Park Service wilderness permit is required. This is a designated camp rather than the Triumph cross-country zone, so it is a different reservation from the col — book the one you actually intend to sleep in. Bear canisters are required and campfires are not allowed; there is a composting toilet.
bivy.capacity: Three individual sites, each capped at a party of four.

bivy.name: The Triumph col
bivy.notes: The standard high camp, on the col northwest of the middle lake, gained by about 1,200 ft of steep talus and grass above the lakes — roughly seven and a half miles and 4,200 ft from the car. Flat ground, running water and a view straight into the Pickets. Published elevations disagree by about 150 ft, from roughly 5,750 to 5,900 ft, so do not plan an altitude-sensitive turnaround off a single figure. A rockier perch just below the col is also used and is well liked.
bivy.water: Snowmelt — a small stream running off the snowpack, and pools near the sites; parties who want more drop toward the stream at the foot of the nearby snowfield. Every published description is of meltwater, and none says when it fails, so treat it as unreliable once the snow has gone.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, in the Triumph cross-country zone: maximum party of six, and only two permits issued per night, which makes it one of the harder zones to get. It is one of the few zones that can be reserved in advance; roughly 40% of capacity is held back for walk-ups issued the day before or the day of, from the Wilderness Information Center at Marblemount. Cross-country camping is allowed only on durable ground — snow, rock or bare earth.
bivy.capacity: Several good bivy spots on and just north of the col — nobody has had to drop to the glacier for want of ground. The real limit is the permit: the Triumph zone takes two parties a night, six people each.

bivy.name: On-ridge bivy above the notch
bivy.notes: Small sites on the crest a hundred to two hundred feet above the notch, one or two pitches up the Northeast Ridge. Parties use them to shorten the climbing day, at the cost of carrying a full day's water onto the ridge. Several trip reports pass through them at dawn rather than sleep there, so treat the ground as confirmed and the comfort as unknown.
bivy.water: None. Everything comes up from the col with you.
bivy.capacity: A couple of small platforms — a party of two or three, spread out.

access.permit: A wilderness/climbing permit is required for overnight backcountry camping (including the bivy col); obtained through the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount or recreation.gov. The Triumph zone has a limited nightly camping quota.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, roughly half a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
bivy.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

bivy.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites

bivy.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
bivy.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. NOT reachable from the Hannegan Pass trailhead — it must never be treated as an alternative camp on that approach.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet streams are dependable through the season, fed from the glaciers above
bivy.permit: THIS ONE IS DIFFERENT. The approach starts in BRITISH COLUMBIA — up Chilliwack Lake Road and onto the rough Depot Creek spur — and walks south across the international boundary on foot into Washington. There is no port of entry on this route, so the trip raises a genuine customs question in both directions that none of the Hannegan-side approaches do; sort out reporting obligations with the relevant border authorities before going, and carry passports. Once across, the camp is inside North Cascades National Park and a park backcountry permit applies, which is awkward given Marblemount is a long drive away on the other side of the range.
bivy.capacity: Open flat benches with room for several tents; informal, with no built sites, toilet or bear hardware

access.rules: Leave No Trace; follow North Cascades National Park backcountry camping rules. The standard approach crosses the international border on foot at an unmonitored boundary marker (border post 65) — carry a passport or passport card and be aware of legal border-crossing requirements even though there is no staffed checkpoint.

bivy.name: Devil's Dream camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED low camp about five miles in on the Wonderland Trail, in trees below Indian Henry's. Useful mainly as a bail-out or a late-start first night — it is well below the climbing and adds a lot of gain to day two. Reliable water is the reason to stop here.
bivy.water: reliable creek water at camp
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; designated trailside camp
bivy.capacity: designated trailside sites, small

bivy.name: Rock slabs below Pyramid Peak
bivy.notes: PLANNED first camp for the standard two-day ascent, out past Indian Henry's and Mirror Lakes where the maintained tread ends. Open slab ground with running water all around it early in the season; once the snowmelt dries up later in summer the water goes with it. Cross-country zone camping — permit required, and it is the last easy water before the cleaver.
bivy.water: running snowmelt nearby into early summer
bivy.capacity: a few tents on open slabs

bivy.name: Dug platform on the lower-mid cleaver
bivy.notes: PLANNED alternative for parties who run out of daylight low on the cleaver. Reports describe digging in here specifically because the spot felt protected from the rockfall lines running down either side — the lower cleaver is loose choss with real exposure to anything a party above knocks down, so on this route the shelter of the platform is the point rather than the view.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: one tent on a dug platform

bivy.name: Cleaver crest col
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the best ground on the route: a broad saddle on the cleaver crest that is generally out of the rockfall lines, which very little else on this cleaver can claim. No water. Above it the crest includes a knife-edge that has to be scrambled once the snow melts off it, so leaving from here in the dark is easier early season when it is still snow-covered. Some parties instead stop around 10,200 ft, which is also comfortable but leaves more of the crest for summit day.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: one to two tents; platforms stomped or dug into snow

access.fees: $82 per person climbing registration fee (paid via Pay.gov before arrival), plus a $12 per person per night wilderness camping fee during peak season (May 1-Sept 15); each lottery application or permit reservation carries a separate non-refundable $6 fee.
access.notes: How to get it: pay online in advance (pay.gov / recreation.gov), then register in person. Winter (Sept 16–May 21): self-issue at the Paradise Old Station kiosk after paying online. Summer (May 22–Sept 30): no self-issue — register at a Wilderness Information Center (Longmire, Paradise, or White River); roughly half of summer registration slots are held for walk-up, up to 24 hrs ahead. No timed-entry vehicle reservation is in effect for the 2026 season, so park entry itself is first-come, first-served.
access.rules: Register in and out at a Wilderness Information Center (Longmire WIC is closest to this route); human waste must be packed out (blue-bag/WAG-bag) above roughly 10,000 ft.
access.permit: Both a Climbing Registration and a Wilderness Permit are required for travel above ~10,000 ft or on any glacier. In summer (May 22-Sept 30), permits are issued only at Wilderness Information Centers (no self-registration kiosks); walk-up permits become available 24 hours before your climb date if not reserved in advance online. Climbers must be 18+ (or have guardian permission), and solo climbing is prohibited without a separate authorized solo permit.
access.closures: West Side Road is closed to vehicle traffic beyond Dry Creek (mile 3) due to repeated Tahoma Creek washouts/slides — open to foot and bike traffic past that gate. The Kautz Creek Trail has been reported closed about a mile from its trailhead due to a large washout; check current NPS alerts before relying on it for access.
access.landManager: Mount Rainier National Park (National Park Service)
access.land_manager: National Park Service
access.parking_pass: Not a Northwest Forest Pass (that's a USFS pass and doesn't apply inside the park). Standard NPS entrance fee applies: $30/vehicle (7 consecutive days), $55 Mount Rainier annual pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.

bivy.name: Boston Basin high camp
bivy.notes: The upper of the basin's two camps, around 6,400 ft, with a composting toilet. It is the natural base for the Quien Sabe: the glacier starts more or less at the tent door, so summit day is short. Snow lingers here well into July, and the rule to pitch only on hardened ground matters — the meadows recover very slowly.
bivy.water: Meltwater streams off the Quien Sabe Glacier and the snowfields above the basin; strongest early in the season and thinner by late summer
bivy.permit: A North Cascades backcountry permit is required, and camping in the basin is legal only at the two designated sites. Permits are picked up in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount and carry a per-person fee plus a reservation fee; demand outstrips supply on peak weekends
bivy.capacity: A designated cluster of hardened sites shared with everyone climbing Forbidden, Sharkfin and Boston — it fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Boston Basin low camp
bivy.notes: Around 5,300 ft on the edge of a moraine crest among small trees, below the polished slabs the Quien Sabe has left behind. Melts out earlier and is more sheltered than the high camp, at the cost of an extra thousand feet on summit morning.
bivy.water: Creeks draining the basin run past the camp through the climbing season
bivy.permit: Same park backcountry permit and the same designated-sites-only rule as the high camp
bivy.capacity: The second designated site, with its own composting toilet; a fallback when the upper sites are taken

bivy.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
bivy.notes: A planned camp and one of the highest in the park, where the maintained trail ends: flat gravel tent pads built onto rock mounds at the foot of the glacier, each ringed by a primitive dry-stone wall, plus a composting toilet. Those walls are there because the site is completely exposed to wind and weather with nothing above it. About six miles and 3,600 ft from the trailhead, and it puts the glacier and the summit pyramid within a short morning.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns at the glacier toe early to mid season; many of these dry up by late summer, so a late-season party should expect to melt snow or carry water up from lower down
bivy.permit: A national park backcountry permit is required and the camp is strictly quota'd — an early-access lottery runs in March and roughly 40% of permits are held for walk-ups, picked up at the wilderness information centre in Marblemount
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites, four people to a site, four parties a night

bivy.name: Doubtful Lake
bivy.notes: The lower fallback, roughly a mile and a thousand feet down a signed spur off the arm. It has water when the high camp does not and it is far more sheltered in bad weather, at the cost of re-gaining that thousand feet to rejoin the route. bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

bivy.name: Clear Creek Campground
bivy.notes: Small campground on the Sauk River a few miles southeast of Darrington on the Mountain Loop Highway, sitting essentially at the mouth of the Clear Creek road that serves Three O'Clock Rock, Exfoliation Dome and Green Giant Buttress. That position is the whole appeal — you can be at the Eightmile trailhead within twenty minutes of leaving camp. Vault toilets only, no water, and twelve sites go quickly on summer weekends.
bivy.water: No potable water on site — carry your own or treat from the river
bivy.permit: Standard Forest Service nightly fee, bookable through Recreation.gov; typically open May through September. No climbing or wilderness permit needed.
bivy.capacity: 12 single sites, vehicles to about 40 ft

bivy.name: Dispersed roadside camping, Clear Creek Road
bivy.notes: Climbers routinely sleep in a vehicle or throw a tent down at a pullout on the Clear Creek road rather than pay for a site, and the trailhead turnaround at the end of the drivable road is the usual spot. This is dispersed camping in the ordinary national forest sense — no fee, no reservation, no permit — which is the practical difference between here and the North Cascades park zones just up the valley. Campfire bans are common from midsummer onward and are worth confirming before you plan on one. No facilities of any kind, so pack out everything including waste.
bivy.water: Creeks near the road most of the season, but nothing developed — filter or treat everything
bivy.permit: NO camping permit required for dispersed camping on national forest land; general forest rules apply (14-day stay limit, camp within about 150 ft of the road, 100 ft from water). A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to PARK at the Eightmile trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Informal pullouts and the trailhead turnaround; a handful of parties at most

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
bivy.capacity: A few parties, informal

bivy.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
bivy.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.
bivy.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need
bivy.permit: None

bivy.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
bivy.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
bivy.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and several parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

bivy.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
bivy.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
bivy.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
bivy.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.permit: No permit required for day scrambling; the upper route brushes the boundary of the adjoining Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness
access.closures: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) is gated for winter, typically closing in early December and reopening mid-to-late April at Washington Pass and Rainy Pass depending on snowpack and avalanche hazard — the peak is inaccessible by car during that window; check WSDOT mountain pass reports before a shoulder-season trip
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District — 24 West Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA; (509) 996-4000
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful pass recommended
